Adjusted assessment incorporating SLOOS:

- The FOMC’s January 26, 2022 statement remains constructive on growth and jobs and signals imminent tightening (ending net asset purchases by early March and preparing to raise the policy rate) while noting elevated inflation and virus-related uncertainty.
- The latest SLOOS reads as broadly supportive for near-term activity: banks report easing standards across C&I and many CRE categories, citing improved economic outlook, competition, strong liquidity, and solid capital positions. Demand for C&I credit strengthened across large, middle-market, and small firms, with more inquiries for credit lines and customer investment needs. Banks also expect improvements in business lending (non-syndicated C&I, syndicated non-leveraged loans, CRE, construction, and land development), consistent with ongoing capex and hiring.
- Offsetting signals: banks reported weaker demand for residential real estate loans (including GSE-eligible and subprime mortgages) and, despite some easing in consumer credit standards, expect deterioration in household credit (credit card, auto, and nonconforming jumbo) as interest rates rise. Foreign banks reported C&I demand roughly unchanged, which tempers breadth.
- Layering in the FSR lens: vulnerabilities persist (stretched valuations, liquidity mismatches in funds, Treasury market fragility under stress, some nonbank leverage, and pockets of CRE risk). Faster tightening could tighten financial conditions and spill over to EMEs.

Net: Compared with the FSR-only view, SLOOS tilts the balance modestly more positive due to easier bank standards and stronger business loan demand, but household credit risks and weaker mortgage demand constrain the upside.
